title: Explain system and network architecture concepts in security operations
tip: This objective is an acronym wall (MFA, SSO, PAM, CASB, PKI, DLP...). Don't just memorize expansions — know what problem each one solves, since questions test application, not spelling.
checklist: Log ingestion: time sync, logging levels
OS concepts: Windows Registry, system hardening, file structure, processes
Network architecture: on-prem/cloud/hybrid, segmentation, zero trust, SASE, SDN
IAM: MFA, SSO, federation, PAM, passwordless, CASB
Sensitive data: DLP, PII, cardholder data (CHD)

title: Analyze indicators of potentially malicious activity
tip: Core SOC-analyst muscle memory and heavily PBQ-tested. Practice sorting a given symptom into network- vs. host- vs. application-related before you try to name the attack.
checklist: Network indicators: bandwidth spikes, beaconing, rogue devices, scans/sweeps, unusual ports
Host indicators: CPU/memory/drive spikes, unauthorized software, malicious processes, registry/file changes
Application indicators: anomalous activity, new accounts, unexpected output, service interruption

title: Use appropriate tools or techniques to determine malicious activity
tip: Email header analysis (SPF vs. DKIM vs. DMARC) is the single most commonly confused trio in this domain — know what each one actually validates, not just the acronym.
checklist: Email analysis: header, DKIM, DMARC, SPF, impersonation
Scripting: Python, PowerShell, regex, JSON, XML

title: Compare and contrast threat-intelligence and threat-hunting concepts
tip: Threat actor types (APT vs. nation-state vs. hacktivist vs. insider) get blended together — anchor each to motive (financial, ideological, espionage, disgruntlement) rather than capability alone.
checklist: Threat actor types: APT, hacktivist, organized crime, nation-state, script kiddie, insider, supply chain
OSINT sources: social media, CERT, CSIRT, deep/dark web
Closed sources: paid feeds, information sharing orgs
Threat hunting: IoCs, honeypots, active defense

title: Explain the importance of efficiency and process improvement in security operations
tip: Lower-yield, mostly conceptual — this is 'why automate' rather than 'how to automate.' Don't overinvest study time here relative to its share of a 33%-weighted domain.

title: Implement vulnerability scanning methods and concepts
tip: The paired terms here (credentialed vs. non-credentialed, agent vs. agentless, active vs. passive) are the classic confusion set — build a single comparison table instead of studying each term in isolation.
checklist: Asset discovery: map scans, device fingerprinting
Passive vs. active, static vs. dynamic (fuzzing)
Frameworks: PCI DSS, CIS benchmarks, OWASP, ISO 27000

title: Analyze output from vulnerability assessment tools
tip: Named tools get swapped constantly (Nessus vs. OpenVAS vs. Burp Suite vs. Nmap) — tie each one to its specific job: network scanner, web app scanner, or vulnerability scanner, not just 'a security tool.'
checklist: Web app scanners: Burp Suite, ZAP, Nikto
Cloud tools: Scout Suite, Prowler, Pacu

title: Analyze data to prioritize vulnerabilities
tip: CVSS scoring is the highest-yield, highest-confusion topic in this whole exam. Know what each metric (attack vector, complexity, privileges required, user interaction, scope, impact) actually measures — students who memorize the score bands without the metrics guess wrong on scenario questions.
checklist: CVSS: attack vector, complexity, privileges required, user interaction, scope

title: Recommend controls to mitigate attacks and software vulnerabilities
tip: The control-type grid (managerial/operational/technical crossed with preventative/detective/responsive/corrective) is easy to blur — practice classifying a real control on both axes at once, not one axis at a time.
checklist: Control function: preventative, detective, responsive, corrective
Patch & config management: testing, rollback, validation
Risk treatment: accept, transfer, avoid, mitigate
Attack surface management: edge/passive discovery, pentesting, bug bounty

title: Explain concepts related to vulnerability response, handling, and management
tip: XSS (reflected vs. persistent), LFI vs. RFI, and SSRF vs. CSRF are the recurring confused pairs here — for each pair, anchor on where the attack executes and who triggers it.
checklist: Secure coding: input validation, output encoding, session management, parameterized queries

title: Explain concepts related to attack methodology frameworks
tip: Cyber kill chain, Diamond Model, and MITRE ATT&CK all describe attacker behavior but from different angles — know which framework you'd reach for to answer 'what phase are we in' vs. 'who/what/where' vs. 'what technique was used.'

title: Perform incident response activities
tip: This is the operational core of the exam — detection/analysis vs. containment/eradication/recovery is a clean sequence, but practice it end-to-end on a real scenario rather than studying the phases as a list.
checklist: Detection/analysis: IoCs, evidence acquisition, chain of custody, data integrity
Containment/eradication/recovery: scope, impact, isolation, remediation, re-imaging

title: Explain the preparation and post-incident activity phases of the incident management life cycle
tip: Straightforward bookends to 3.2 — preparation happens before an incident, post-incident activity happens after. Don't let root cause analysis and lessons learned blur together; one asks why, the other asks what changes.
checklist: Preparation: IR plan, playbooks, tabletop exercises, training, BC/DR
Post-incident: forensic analysis, root cause analysis, lessons learned

title: Explain the importance of vulnerability management reporting and communication
tip: Often under-studied because it feels like common sense — it isn't tested that way. Know the specific components of a vuln management report, not just that reports exist.
checklist: Vuln mgmt reporting: affected hosts, risk score, mitigation, recurrence, prioritization
Inhibitors to remediation: MOU, SLA, legacy/proprietary systems

title: Explain the importance of incident response reporting and communication
tip: MTTD vs. MTTR (respond) vs. MTTR (remediate) is a genuinely confusing near-acronym-collision — write out what each one measures in plain English before trying to memorize the abbreviation.
checklist: IR report structure: executive summary, who/what/when/where/why, timeline, impact, scope, evidence
Legal, PR, regulatory, law enforcement communication
Metrics: mean time to detect, respond, remediate; alert volume
